utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please be so kind to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the cross-examination of the witness, I'd like to remind you that the Court still has to take a decision on Document P2171, which is the redacted translation of the report that was tendered last Friday, especially the English translation. Since you were not there, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we waited with this decision since it concerns an English text so that whenever there are any objections, that they could be made. So may I remind you to that, if there are any objections to be made, that it should be done by today. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, apart from that, I see that you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you. I am going to examine the first point and to state the position of the Defence. Thank you in advance. I'd like to say, Mr. President, that we have had an agreement with the Prosecution -- we reached it a moment ago -- with respect to a question linked to the translation of the documents that are relevant to this particular witness, Mr. Dzonko, and this translation, with respect to the black box -- that we termed black box and white box. And I should like to be authorised to give me three minutes to say something at the end of the cross-examination. May I be accorded three minutes, because we did reach an agreement, myself and Mr. Ierace, on one particular point. Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be glad to grant you three minutes in order to inform us about an agreement between the parties. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'll ask to the registrar in Sarajevo to bring in Mr. Dzonko again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzonko. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzonko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to see that you are there, and also good to see that you're wearing your glasses. Thank you very much for bringing them. Mr. Dzonko, may I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday. Now, the cross-examination by counsel for the Defence will resume. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dzonko. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. We stopped off yesterday when we were talking about -- and could you confirm this -- that one of your daughters was called Mrs. Golo. Is that right? Is your daughter's name Mrs. Golo?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We were discussing the question of soldiers, actually, and you said that you saw some soldiers belonging to the Bosnian army, that is to say, the Sarajevo army, round about, in the environs. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now, with respect to the passage -- and when I use the word "passage," I am referring to what you yourself indicated as being the passage or passageway between two blocks of houses, residential blocks. Now, in respect of that passage, do you know where the army that you call the Sarajevo army was located? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There seems to be some noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you understood the question? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an answer, please.

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where they were, where the army was. I just saw them going to the kitchen. On their way to the kitchen, I would see one or two of them passing by, without any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have just told me that at the front line, the soldiers weren't carrying arms, weren't armed. Am I right in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they had weapons or not at the front line, I don't know, but when they were on their way to the kitchen, then they went walking in a normal fashion, a normal way, ordinary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the front lines were 50 metres away from your apartment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts. Fifty or sixty perhaps, metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, you said in one of your statements that you gave to the interviewers that you could see the soldiers and that you could know whether they were wearing uniforms or whether they were not in uniform; is that correct? You could see that?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you also said in one of your statements, the one that we were examining yesterday, that you were aware of the fact that the army were in an apartment, had premises in an apartment block near your own. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "close by," close to your apartment block, what do you mean by "close"? How close?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would see them passing by on their way to breakfast, to have breakfast or lunch. When there was a ceasefire, when there was no shooting, I would see some of them walking past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, to go back to your statement, how far away were these premises where the army was from your apartment? Could you give us an idea in metres? What distance would you say it was?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about 100 to 150 metres. I heard them there, because they were moving through the trenches, the connecting trenches, so you couldn't really see them very well, but you could see them entering and leaving the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt? I hear that here in the courtroom we have -- it seems to have a loudspeaker on in the original language, which is not of great assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware that the loudspeaker was switched on, Mr. President. I do apologise, and thank you for intervening. Thank you, Mr. Usher, as well, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated to us the presence of military trenches. Now, these trenches, could you see them from your apartment? Could you see the trenches?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you know where they were?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that either, because I wasn't able to go into that part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you saw a number of photographs. Do you remember the photographs? Do you remember seeing them?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on the photographs that you were shown, could you see the area and premises of the army that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, may I have your assistance again, please. I should like you to place on the ELMO a photograph, and the number of the photograph is -- the last digits are 35, from a series of photographs. I think that the registrar can provide you with those photographs. It is a photograph which shows residential blocks, with the headquarters. Would you please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see these apartment blocks now on the photograph which is on your screen, Witness? Can you see that photograph and those --

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see anything. I don't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] I need the assistance of the technical booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or perhaps should the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Your Honour, we do not have the image on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask the assistance of the technical booth in order to take care that the image we see on our screen now will also be seen on the screen in Sarajevo. Ms. Philpott, you still are not able to see on the screen in Sarajevo, the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] That's correct, Your Honour. We do not have the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even under another button or...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Your Honour, now we have the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just received the confirmation that the picture is on the screen in Sarajevo now. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Would you please use your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry for that, sir. [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think you can now see the photograph. It is number 1212/36 -- 35, sorry. Can you see it properly?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in one or other of the buildings that we see on the photograph, the residential blocks, at the time that we are discussing -- at the material time, that is to say, the summer of 1992 to the summer of 1994, were there premises that were used by the Sarajevo army in those houses, as you call them the Sarajevo army?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you said that you were living with your son-in-law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, your son-in-law at that time, was he called to the colours?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he worked in Unioninvest. He was at Bembasa, but he was called up, but he was working at Bembasa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was your son-in-law incorporated in the army? Was he called up?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, your son-in-law at that time, was he called to fight? Was he called up to fight, to engage in combat?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was -- while he was incorporated in the army, where did your son-in-law sleep?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does that mean where you yourself lived? In that house, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not there at that time. I only came to Trnovac, and when I arrived, then they came to fetch him from Unioninvest to go and work at the Bambesa. And he worked there for two or three years until the liberation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked at the Unioninvest with water, for those -- for that water which was there. And he worked there, and he was the boss there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does that mean to organise the distribution of water in Sarajevo? Is that what he did?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your son-in-law was active during two or three years of the war, is it?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when he was dealing with this water, engaged with water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Do you know if your daughter, who is now called Mrs. Golo, that she also gave a statement to OTP investigators? Did she give a statement? When we speak about Mrs. Golo, is that the person that you live with? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. You are saying that you could not see the trenches. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I never dared go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring, Witness, to those near your apartment.

utterances.speaker: RASID DJONKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. One could not see them because it was to the left. I don't know how many metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. I will now read out to you the statement which your daughter made. I will read it in Serbian, and I apologise in advance, but I hope you will understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I shall be very happy to place a copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume that my learned colleague proposes to contradict some aspect of this witness's evidence with something from a statement. Perhaps he could indicate in advance which part of Ms. Golo's statement he proposes to read in that regard. He could refer, perhaps, to the relevant paragraph. Because if it is on the point that the trenches can or cannot be seen from the apartment, I'm unsure as to what part of Ms. Golo's statement it could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please inform Mr. Ierace, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, on which part you're about to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be happy to do that, but I do not know if the witness can hear us. But I can say that because -- so that Mr. Ierace can find it. Mr. Ierace will find it like this: It is Document Number ERN 0303-4033 [as interpreted], and it is the Serbian text which I have before me. So will you please take it up, Mr. Ierace, the second sentence in the passage beginning with the word "night," or "the night," or "during the night." Do you have this text before you, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the text be placed on the ELMO, please, in some language so that interpreters know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, I ask that Mr. Piletta-Zanin simply indicate the paragraph as well as the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Third paragraph, second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before I was interrupted, I was about to read you a sentence, and I will read it in Serbian. I apologise, but if necessary, we can place it on the screen so that with your eyeglasses you can read it as well as I will, and I will wait that this be done so that you can read it. It is the second sentence of the third passage: "At night -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The appropriate procedure is simply for my friend to read the sentence rather than place the whole paragraph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness testified yesterday that he could decipher letter by letter a text and then finally he would be able to put together a few letters to words. So please, if you did not provide the interpreters' booth, would you just read very slowly the part you are putting to the witness, and I don't think it's of any use to put it on the ELMO at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is exactly what I was about to do. Usher, will you please put the text on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I said it would be of no use to put it on the ELMO if you read the line slowly in the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So I'm quoting the second sentence in the third passage, which reads as follows,

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: which were returned from Bosnian trenches." Thank you for the perfect interpretation into French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear this sentence?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard it, but did you also understand it?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Why, yes, I did, but I was never on that side, because after I was wounded, I kept keeping to this other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please not speak over the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when the witness is talking, would you please wait, unless there's a good reason to stop him, but just then leave it to ask him to stop, and nothing else, otherwise the interpreters cannot follow us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, is it correct that your daughter could see, at night, the gunfire, and that this gunfire was returned from Bosnian trenches? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: It is true. She could see it, because she slept on the right side, downstairs. And I was with the children, next to the street. I had to look after the children so they don't get away, and I, therefore, could not see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you are telling us that throughout these events which interest us, that is, during those two -- that is, three years -- 1992, 1993, 1994 -- you never went into the room where your daughter slept so as to see the trenches?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: I could not see them, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The relevant passage refers to night-time --

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- and bullets being seen at night-time. It is not a decisive passage to the effect that the trenches themselves could be seen, especially at night. Therefore, the question put to the witness misrepresents the passage from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please rephrase the question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were about to tell me, is that correct, that you never had an opportunity during the three years that we are talking about to go into the room in question or next to the room in question at any time?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: I could go there, and I did, but when there was gunfire, I didn't know where it was coming from, from one side or the other, but I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you went to that side, to that wing of the apartment, could you see the trenches that your daughter saw living there, or not?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, why couldn't you see the trenches if your daughter could see them from that same place?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I make the same objection. The witness, the deponent to this statement, is clearly referring to tracer fire because she refers to bullets being fired at night. She does not state explicitly that she saw the trenches from which the fire came. That may well have been a presumption on her part, and therefore again my learned colleague is not entitled to -- presumption to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained. Would you please keep this in mind, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Serb text of this witness says expressly -- and I have it before me and I will read it. It reads explicitly that one could see the fire which was returned from Serb trenches, and it is mentioned in the Serb text from Bosnian trenches. And this witness, Golo, who is not still a witness but might be, she is confirming the presence of trenches, and contrary to what Mr. Ierace is saying, this -- in this statement, this was an explicit reference to trenches which this witness said that she had seen, at least in Serbian language. I do not know whether this will affect your decision, or do you still sustain the objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you quoted yourself, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the statement of Ms. Golo you quoted was that one could see the fire which was returned from Serb trenches. Your interpretation of this line is, although the text doesn't say that, that she could see the trenches from which fire was returned, which is a different thing, and I -- the line as such does not clearly indicate how Ms. Golo knew that the source of the fire was from the trenches. It does not explicitly say that she could see the trenches when the fire was returned. So the decision will remain the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said, and I think repeated several times, that in that area fighting was a daily occurrence. Is that correct? Can you confirm it for us?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, still in relation to the fighting, you said that the soldiers that you saw, that some of those soldiers that you saw wore uniforms and others didn't. Can you please confirm this.

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you mean "some yes and some no"? What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: They didn't have any uniforms. I guess that is. I wouldn't know. I didn't ask them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers, if I understand you well, who were active-duty soldiers, they did not have uniforms? Is that how I should understand you?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Witness, we shall now put on the ELMO with the help of the usher here in The Hague a photograph which is 1211/34A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this photograph on the ELMO. I could give you my own copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you will see -- at least I hope so -- a photograph which represents the view from your kitchen. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you said that yesterday and you pointed that you had been wounded on your left-hand side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the bullet had come from the passage that one can see far away, slightly to the left of the centre in that photograph. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the bullet went through the carpentry element before it hit you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French interpretation was perfect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the bullet went through the carpentry element, the door frame, it hit you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: No, it is not. It hit the wall and then ricochetted from the wall, and that is how it hit me on the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I now want to move on to a different series of questions. Witness, are you aware of a school in the vicinity of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: No. No -- oh, yes. Children went to the cellar behind our building to the left. That is where they went. But the school, no. The school was far away in the Serb...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. You said, I believe at the time of your earlier statement, that you were perfectly acquainted with the place from which the bullets -- the bullet could have come, the bullet that hit you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you say that the bullet came from the Faculty of Theology?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Because it couldn't have come from anywhere else. That was the only possible place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you lose anyone close to you during the war because of the war?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Well, you know, I lost my brother, two sons-in-law, a grandchild, and very many other relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, don't you feel resentful, bitter, now?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Well, of course one cannot forget what one's lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how could you be so emphatic and affirm categorically that the bullet came from the Faculty of Theology?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Well, you know what everybody says, and I always said, that it couldn't have come from anywhere else except there at that height because it must have been fired from the roof because that is how it travelled. Otherwise, it wouldn't have hit that way, reached the target that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true that you said in one of your statements that in the beginning, you had been told by somebody that a bullet could have come from the Faculty of Theology?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Well, it was in this direction, between the buildings. Of course, we are assuming. I'm not affirming that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was the following: Isn't it true that you were told that a bullet could have come from the Faculty of Theology?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd be grateful if my friend could refer me to the statement by its date and by its page and by its paragraph before the witness answers that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the source, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do it right away, Mr. President. I'm trying to find my way between the English and the Serbian text so as to give you the -- an exact answer. Just a moment. Meanwhile, I will ask you a different series of questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to confirm to us a document which was shown you yesterday and which was this "discharge from the hospital" document which you saw about ten days ago for the first time, that is, at least what you said. That is at least what you said yesterday during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness did not say that he saw the document for the first time ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please indicate where the witness testified that it was ten days ago that he saw the document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall, Mr. President, that that is what the witness said yesterday during the direct examination. Do you want me to look for the exact line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The line, Mr. President, yesterday is page 5674, and I am reading the English but I was listening to the Serbian, so my recollection might be slightly different. The question was: [In English] "And when have you seen it before?" [Interpretation] And to that question, the answer was as follows: [In English] "Ten days ago."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I assume that you understood the objection of Mr. Ierace. Your question was that he saw it for the first time ten days ago. That was what your question was about. The witness said that he has seen it ten days before, but not that that was the first time that he saw it. At least, not in the line you indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the very next question and answer I think will clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question was: "All right. And before then, had you seen it? In other words, apart from ten days ago, had you seen it before?" "I don't remember. Maybe I forgot." That's what it says. So that confirms again that at least it's not the testimony of the witness that he saw it for the first time ten days ago. So the objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. It is quite possible that the witness has indeed forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are putting to the witness that he testified that he saw it for the first time ten days ago. There's an objection against that. There's no reason to comment on it any more. It's not what the witness testified. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comment whatsoever, Mr. President. Thank you. May I confer with my colleague, please, five seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to go back to the statement and the portion quoted yesterday. It was a statement, and the number of it was 0090-8226. And the date of it was the 13th of November, 1994 -- 9-5, I'm sorry. 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that statement, you said that they indicated to you that the bullet came from that direction. Now, Witness, do you confirm the statement you made on the 13th of November, 1995, and the statement was given to Mr. Jan Van Hecke?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll withdraw my objection at this stage, given the last few words of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I see that after all this time that we've lost, the objection has been retracted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Witness, could you tell us, yes or no, do you confirm it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, confirm what? The question asked earlier started off with the proposition which is not an accurate reflection of the statement. It then was refined to whether he confirms that he made a statement on a particular date and that the statement was given to a particular investigator. So perhaps he could clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please clarify since the question, as it reads from the transcript, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. My question before the interruption made and retracted by Mr. Ierace was: "You said that you were told that the bullet came from the area quoted, that is to say, the Faculty of Theology."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Took us a long time. Witness, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Well, everybody who was standing there. Actually, it couldn't have come from any other direction than from the direction where the theological faculty is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer, but am I right in saying that this assertion on your part, this affirmation, is only what you heard people say, what you heard other people say? Is that right? Am I right in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take a moment to confer, Mr. President, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we've finished with this witness. I would like three more minutes, but after the witness, if I may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, I've got one question for you.

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You repeatedly told us that the bullet could not have come from any other source than from the Faculty of Theology.

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also testified that other people told you that it should have been from the Faculty of Theology that the bullet came from.

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are talking about a conclusion as to where the bullet came from. Was this just the conclusion of the other people who told you where the bullet came from or would that also be your own conclusion?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzonko.

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Well, no. I couldn't say. That's what they assume. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And so I do understand you that that's not your assumption but just the assumption of the other people?

utterances.speaker: "At night I would see bullets getting at us from Nedzarici and
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Ierace --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Judge Nieto-Navia has a question for you in relation to the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: My question is the following: This document, 2771, the medical release, which is the one with the dark areas and signed by the witness, this document, was it disclosed to the Defence? If your answer is yes, please tell me when.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was disclosed twice. It was first disclosed on the 8th of June, 2000, and on the second occasion, on the 6th of November, 2001. I'm sorry. The 26th of November, 2001 was the second occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes your examination as a witness in this Court. I thank you very much for coming, especially also for returning today after you spent already quite some time yesterday. You will understand that it's important for this Court to hear the answers to questions put by both parties to the witnesses while preparing for the decisions that we'll have to take.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming. You are released now as a witness. Ms. Philpott, we'll need a couple of minutes in The Hague before the examination of the next witness will start. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the three minutes, would that be prior to our decisions on the -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, with respect to the documents and the question raised by Judge Nieto-Navia a moment ago, to draw your -- tell you the following: To copy two sets of documents, because it is necessary for us to know exactly what the Chamber is confronted with. So I suggest that I circulate these two sets of documents. We have them for the Defence, for the Registry and the Trial Chamber. It is always the same document, one in the black copy, dark copy, and one in the light copy, with the translations attached. The reason for my intervention, you will understand it, because a moment ago, when you had these documents before you, I took the liberty of underlining certain elements, just to draw the attention of the Chamber and to save time. May I now be authorised to submit these two pieces and provide copies for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Usher, may I have your assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, I have copies for the Chamber as well. [In English] Bring the copies to the attention the Chamber, of course. One is for the -- yes. One is for the Prosecution and ...to the attention of the Chamber. Yes. [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether you have these elements now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to the attention of the Chamber and the Prosecution. We should have two sets of documents, in fact, Mr. President. The first is the dark version, the black version, with the translation behind it, following, which is the shortest, the briefest of translations; and secondly, we have the better copy, followed by the translation, which is the longer of the two translations. Now, if we have all these documents, a copy of the original and a copy of the translation, if we all have that, may I now continue? Do we have it? Do all the parties have those documents now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that I got one set stapled and the other one loose. Yes. I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, quite, but we prepared the documents very properly for the usher and I see that the usher has the documents in his hands. We did prepare it very correctly and properly. Thank you. I see that Mr. Ierace is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fairness to the Defence, I should withdraw something I said earlier. The question posed to me was when the Prosecution first disclosed the dark copy which bore the signature of the witness, and I then gave two dates. The first date was the 8th of June, 2000, and the second date was the 26th of November, 2001. The first date I took -- both dates I took from the sheet which is in the possession of the Trial Chamber and the Defence, that is, the sheet of potential exhibits of witnesses, and in particular, the copy that was forwarded on the 13th of March, 2002. I note that the first date relates to a particular set of ERN numbers which appears on both the versions of the dark copy, that is, the version signed by the witness and the version unsigned by the witness. The second ERN number, which relates to the date of the 26th of November, 2001, is the copy which has two ERN numbers on it and which contains a signature. The version which has only one ERN number on it, which is the first ERN number, does not have a signature. Therefore, on the basis of that information, I can confidently say that the first date, the document with the witness's signature, was disclosed was the 26th of November, 2001. However, I add this: that the Defence has been served with a statement by the witness which is dated the 13th of November, 1995. That document is signed by the witness. The version signed by the witness commences with ERN number 0036-1008. The statement ends with 0036-1010. Your Honours will note that the second ERN number on the medical report signed by the witness and dated the 13th of November is 0036-1011, in other words, the next consecutive number. In other words, it was processed by the evidence unit on the same occasion as the statement signed on the 13th of November, 1995. The relevance of all of that is it seems that the witness signed this document at the same time that he signed his statement, and of course that was the same day of the month and the same month, although the year was not included alongside his signature on the photocopy of the letter of discharge. So while I withdraw that date of the 8th of June, 2000, I also point out that the documentary evidence strongly, if not overwhelmingly, suggests that he placed his signature on a letter of discharge on the 13th of November, 1995. Given the witness's obvious poor state of recollection, it is inappropriate to pursue that with the witness in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, after we heard the explanation about the different versions of this document, please proceed because you would like to draw our attention to other aspects --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I should like to thank the Prosecution for all those technical and detailed pieces of information but which have nothing to do with the problem in hand. Having said that, I'm going to show you why now. Mr. President, you now have two copies of the same document. We all agree on that score, never mind the signature at the end of Witness Dzonko. We're not interested in that for the moment. But you have before you, Mr. President, two translations at the back of the documents. One has an ERN number 0073-2936. Let me repeat. 73-2936, with other ERN numbers, but that was the most important ERN number. We have three ERN numbers actually. And the other document is the one that is Exhibit P2771.1. Mr. President, I think we agree that this is one and the same document in two versions, whether it be a black version and a white version. But the square, the top square, that we can see, the top box which is printed out, is the same in both versions. I think that is clear. But when you compare the two translations, Mr. President, of one and the same document, we come to one surprise after another. And that is the reason why the Defence has asked for the production -- always asked for the production of the original. Let me explain. The box that we have in the document that is 73-2936 is the same as the one that appears in the top part of the other document, P2771.1. Now, I underlined for your own information, Mr. President, the differences that are unacceptable. I say "unacceptable" for the following reasons: Because some things don't exist quite simply. For example, the term "surgical" does not figure anywhere in the other document. Maybe on the stamps but not on the document proper. Then, there is additional information. But above all, what I should like to draw the Chamber's attention to is the following: If we take Document 73-2936 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Are you comparing these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At a distance, I think I am. I'm speaking of the two translations actually, Judge. These two translations, one translation and the other translation. I can't see that far. I have to take up my glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here 2936. I have a document which is numbered 2936.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, that's this one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other one is P2771.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge. That is correct. Now, as we have these two documents, let me draw your attention, Mr. President, to the following: The bottom half of 2936, it has indications which are not present either in the translation, 2771, or in any of the two other documents -- copies of the document, whether it's the black version or the white version. Now, if we look at the last box, it says "result of treatment." You have a box where it says "result of treatment" in the 2936 version. You'll be able to see that there are eight points. Now, these eight points correspond simply to the six points -- or rather six boxes or squares which are at the bottom of the pre-printed form which begins with -- which you'll be able to find, Mr. President, the last little box on the left, and we see six, whereas in the translation there are eight points. Points 5 and 7 apparently do not exist. And even better than that, Mr. President, you will see that in the translation that we received at the time, which was the 73-296 [sic] one, there is a sentence at the bottom of that box, and I'm going to read it out. It is as follows; this is what it says: [In English] "For medical examinations, please report to the surgical department of this clinic, Brasova Street, Sarajevo." And you'll be able to see that that line, Mr. President, does not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appear in any of the two documents, whether they are the dark version or the light version, which were given to us by the Prosecution, whether they were given directly to the witness in Sarajevo or the clear copy that we had. Now, in other words, when we note that the translation that I have furnished with these three ERN numbers incorporate elements of the pre-printed text which do not exist in any of the other texts and copies of the original given -- provided by the Prosecution, this can only signify one thing, and that is that other documents were handed up for translation, documents which incorporated elements and information which was supplementary and cannot be found either in the dark version or the light version, Mr. President. I think that that is the only conclusion that one can arrive at reasonably and logically to which I draw your attention. And it is absolutely imperative for the Prosecution to provide the originals so that we can know which and what they are, and so that the Chamber itself and the Defence, of course, does not have to work with translations which are translations done on the basis of other -- apparently other elements, other than the ones that were disclosed to the Chamber in the course of the trial and the proceedings. I apologise for having to bring up these elements and for having to underline them in a coloured ink. But I did so because we're working with the Serbian language and the English language, and I did so so that the Chamber can see the realities that we are facing in terms of translation but also because we do not have the production of original documents. The last number is 936, those are the principal digits, and that particular document includes elements which do not exist in any of the versions, either the dark version or the light version, the poorer version or the better version, of the letter of discharge which was provided by the Prosecution. So that is a problem. And I would like to hear on the spot from Mr. Ierace. Perhaps he can give us a direct answer on the spot; or if not, in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems that there are two principal aspects to the document that my friend has highlighted in support of his theory that the translation -- the translator had documents other than the originals produced by the Prosecution in order to come up with the translations. The first of those, as I understand it, is an observation by my friend that the one translation contains the word "surgical" in the context of surgical department. And to quote his words: "The term `surgical' does not figure anywhere in the other document." That's page 28, line 3. I draw my learned colleague's attention to, firstly, the appearance of the word "surgical" at the top right-hand corner of ERN number, last numbers 8842; and on the other translation, which is last four numbers ERN 2936, at the middle of the box on the second line. Both documents, in fact, have the title "Surgical Department." The second concern he refers to is this: That on the document with the last ERN numbers 2936, we see under the heading "result of treatment," eight possibilities. When one looks at the original that accompanies it, one simply doesn't see at the relevant point the same layout or, in relation to some boxes, that one can discern of the relevant point. One can only see five discrete boxes, perhaps a sixth. The translation which accompanies the clearer version, that is last four ERN numbers 8842, indeed shows six boxes, as can be seen on the clearer photocopy, that is, last ERN numbers 8842. It is crystal clear. And therefore, there is no apparent discrepancy between the clearer original, 8842, and the rough translation of the same ERN number marked Exhibit P2771.1. Mr. President, there is, in my submission, firstly overwhelming evidence available without the assistance of an expert that when one compares the poorer and better copies of the medical discharge summary, that they are one and the same document. And I have not heard my friend at any stage suggest otherwise. That does not seem to be in dispute. That being the case, we now have the benefit of the more legible copy, that is, 8842. And it follows that we have a reliable translation for that part of the original document which is legible. I do not understand my friend to have at any stage suggested that the rough translation of 8842 in any way is inaccurate of the legible parts of the original. So that is not in dispute. That being the case, it seems to me that the way is clear for the document to be tendered, of course, on the understanding that much of the original remains illegible. That which is illegible has not been translated. What, then, is the probative value of the document? It is this: I refer now to the clearly legible portions. It is evidence that on the 17th of July, 1994, Rasid Dzonko, who was born in 1926, was admitted to the University Medical Centre of Sarajevo -- there has been other evidence that that is Kosevo Hospital -- where he received treatment and was discharged 12 days later on the 29th of July, 1994. In other words, it is evidence which is consistent, and therefore, corroborative, of the evidence of Rasid Dzonko from whom we have just heard. Beyond that, there is some decipherable reference to the nature of the injuries for which he received treatment. My friend makes much of the fact that the treating doctor, or at least the doctor who completed the report and signed it, is a gynecologist. In any context other than a city in a three-year siege, that would seem surprising. But it is not in the context of Sarajevo in 1994. Mr. President, as I indicated yesterday, should the Trial Chamber rule that the diagnosis part of the letter of discharge is insufficiently legible for it to be tendered, then I am content for the material which appears in the box, that is, the top half of the document, be tendered and the bottom half to be not tendered. In any event, even if the whole document was rejected, the Trial Chamber still has the direct evidence of the surviving victim himself as to his name, his age, when he was admitted to hospital, when he was discharged, and the reason, especially, why he received treatment. I would not want those last few comments to be interpreted as any lack of confidence on my part as to the appropriateness of the tender, especially of the top half of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you'd like to add something and you could do it briefly, then you could proceed, otherwise we would have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I shall be happy, then, to do that after the break, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you immediately it will take 15 seconds, 15 seconds, not more than that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May I note only this, Mr. President, Your Honours, that we should know why this last line and these last two figures, 5 and 7, were translated when they do not exist in the exhibit, and this question has remained unanswered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you one question, Mr. Ierace: Do you intend to offer any evidence in respect of the authenticity of the document, as we discussed before, under 92 bis? We've seen a lot of documents available, and of course we do not know what finally you'll tender. Would this be one of the documents which was included or would you have to check that during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you mean by that: Is the more legible version coming in through one of the 92 bis witnesses as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- I will check that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, badly legible or well legible, black box or -- well, whatever copy, but I'd like to know whether this is your intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can tell you that I have here at the bar table, should you wish to see it, the originals of both documents, and I'm happy for them to be handed up. When I use the word "original," I mean simply the most original copy which the OTP has ever possessed, that is, the letter of discharge which has a black patch and which has been signed by the witness. So this is the original signing by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I also have the more legible version, that is, the one which was received by the Office of the Prosecutor. Of course, one -- the copy signed -- it seems that the witness signed a photocopy, although of course his signature is original, and the more legible version is clearly not the original document and it appears to be an old photocopy. I hand both of those up. Perhaps they can be shown to my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Then it's time for a break, which gives us the opportunity as well to consider the matter of this document. So we'll not deal with any document at this very moment. We'll do that after the break. Apart from that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are talking about an agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We agreed to discuss this matter before the Chamber at a given time, and that is now, during these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll then adjourn until 10 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before resuming the examination of witnesses, I'd like to inform the parties about the admission into evidence of the documents. Let's perhaps first take the easy part, the photographs. That's document P3279T, as far as I can see, a set of six photographs. Since I didn't hear any objections, they're admitted in evidence. Then we come to the medical report, discharge form of a patient in the clinical university centre of Sarajevo. I gave a provisional decision earlier. The document as it is now, whether it's the badly legible copy or the copy tendered P2771, cannot be admitted at this moment in evidence. If the Prosecution would assist in seeking admission of this document in evidence, it would be minimally required that there is a translation to that document, at least of the legible parts of the document, that can create no confusion in whatever way; that means the type of boxes or the entries in the boxes. So therefore the translations, the two different translations of what seems to be one document, are not acceptable. A further requirement would be that this document, as the Chamber is allowed to ask for and which has been asked for by the Defence as well, that an authentication of this document will be presented to the Chamber. Although there has been no objection to the effect that the Defence has argued that the two copies of the document would not be copies of the same document under the present circumstances and with the confusion the translations have created, the Chamber thinks that it would be necessary to at least have evidence that these copies are in conformity with the originals in Sarajevo or that the originals be produced. Finally, if these requirements would be met, that could only result in an admission into evidence of the upper part of the document, and then only those boxes in which the entries are well legible. The format as it is, the pre-printed parts, all seem to be sufficiently legible. And just to give you an indication, the name of the patient, the year of birth, the number on the form, the date of admission, the date of discharge, and the surgery performed, these entries seem to be fairly legible. And it would only be to that extent that the Chamber, if the other requirements would be met, is willing to admit this document in evidence. Then I think, if no one's on his feet, we could resume the examination of the next witness, Mr. Ierace. It was not an invitation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, but if you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I simply wanted to stand up to thank the Chamber for the decision it took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Ierace, would you please call the next witness. That would be, as far as I can see on my list, Mr. Kapetanovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is the correct name, Mr. President. But before we leave the matter of the previous witness, Rasid Dzonko, I seek to tender the video that was played to the witness. That is P3279TT. And might the documents which were obtained from the evidence vault now be returned so that they can be conveyed back to the evidence vault. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll -- wouldn't it be the wisest that we return all the documents we have just reviewed for preparing our decision with marks, even my marks, on it? That will be then returned. Yes, Madam Registrar, I forgotten about the video. And that shows again that I'd rather leave it in your hands than to do it myself. The video was Number P3279TT, and is admitted into evidence. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to seize this opportunity, because you know the position of the Defence with reference to exhibits. I'm talking about 2171, which is a page like this. There is a part of it which is masked mechanically which we received on Friday, and we're very happy to receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there are no objections in having --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe that that is what I said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The translation partly blackened is also admitted into evidence, and that is 2171. Yes, then, Mr. Ierace, you may call the next witness. Perhaps we could ask the representatives of the Registry in Sarajevo to lead the witness into the videoroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome. I cannot say "in the courtroom," but at least in the videoroom linked to this courtroom. Before giving your testimony, Mr. Kapetanovic, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration is handed out to you now by the representative of the Registry. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kapetanovic. Please be seated. Mr. Kapetanovic, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution; subsequently, you'll be examined by counsel for the Defence; and if there are any additional questions from the Judges, they will be put to you as well. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, would you please spell your surname.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: K-A-P-E-T-A-N-O-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, what is your birthdate?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: 19th February, 1931.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, were you living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you living -- withdraw that. Whereabouts were you living in Sarajevo in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you living with, amongst other people -- withdraw that. In the same apartment block, was there a man by the name of Ivan Franjic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you also know a person by the name of Augustin Vucic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an occasion where you witnessed both those men being injured?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to do it exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, do you remember the year when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: 1993. I think -- I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I believe it was April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing when those two men were injured?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: We were walking along Ante Babica Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it daytime or night-time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Daytime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time of day was it when they were injured?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: About 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were walking in Ante Babica Street. In which direction were you walking in that street?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: We were walking in the direction of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- were the three of you walking in a line or not? In other words, were you walking side by side or not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: In a line, one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that they were injured, who was in the middle of the three of you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Augustin Vucic was in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was on his left?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I was on his left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, therefore, that Ivan Franjic was on his right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason as to why the three of you were walking at that place at about 10.00 in the morning on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: No particular reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you walked along that part of that street before that day during the war?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on this occasion as the three of you walked along that street?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: While we were moving along the street, what happened was that a sniper bullet came and hit two people, Ivan and Vucic, and I wasn't wounded myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the sound of any shots being fired at about the time that Ivan and Augustin were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't hear the sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the bullet touch any part of you or your clothing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part did it touch?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: From the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said that the bullet touched part of either you or your clothing. Which part of you or your clothing did the bullet make contact with?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: The belt on my trousers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was Ivan Franjic injured?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Through the stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was Augustin Vucic wounded?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: He was wounded in the kidney, I think. The kidney, yes. His kidney was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how old was Ivan Franjic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Sixty-five or sixty-seven, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how old was Augustin Vucic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: About 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Augustin Vucic was wounded in the kidney. Did you see which side of his body was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: The left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Ivan Franjic was wounded through the stomach. Was that towards the middle of the stomach or to one side?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: The middle, above his belly button.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say how many shots were fired, given that you did not hear the sound of the shots or shot?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Assuming -- I assume that there was just one bullet, assuming that it was a sniper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, given that you did not hear the sound, are you able to say from which direction the shot or shots were fired?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: From the right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say --

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: -- in the direction in which we were moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis did you form your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of our movement towards Dobrinja, and that's why I considered that the bullet had come from our right, from the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the shooting? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: After the shooting I tried to save Franjic. I tried to get a car, to stop a car that came along first to transport him to the first aid station. He was taken to Dobrinja, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone offer any assistance apart from --

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: A woman came up to us, and a man who gave us some bandages which I tied round his stomach to stop his intestines from coming out. So I was able to tighten this bandage around his stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that Ivan was taken off to Dobrinja in a car. What happened to Augustin?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: When I sent off Ivan to Dobrinja, I tried to help Augustin. And the first car that turned up I stopped to take him to Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Augustin survive the wound?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ivan survive the wound, his wound?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What clothes were you wearing that day, at the time that the shooting occurred?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: An ordinary jacket. We were all wearing ordinary jackets. Windjammers [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of pants were the three of you wearing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Ordinary trousers, the kind we had. Ordinary ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a pensioner, and so was Ivan. He was retired, too. Augustin was just about to become a pensioner as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that Augustin was just about to become a pensioner, do you know what his occupation was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- unofficially, but I think he was a metal worker, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that Ivan and Augustin were shot, was there anyone nearby you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the shooting, was there anyone nearby the group of you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody. Just the three of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any military people in the vicinity at all at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown -- first I ask a map be placed on the ELMO here. That is P3202. And perhaps whilst that is being done, Ms. Philpott could show the same exhibit to the witness in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Philpott, could you please confirm that you have P3202, and that you put it on the ELMO in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour. I have that exhibit, and it is now on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My eyesight isn't very good, and I can't find my way around this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Kapetanovic. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: May I have a photograph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a moment I think you will be handed a map which has a red mark on it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your signature anywhere on that document? I direct your attention to the bottom of the document.
